These concepts have been validated through selected examples featuring unusual polarization transformation effects and exceptional bending of incident waves.

We introduce eCPNN, a deep learning framework designed to solve time-dependent many-body Schrödinger equations across diverse physical systems with varying degrees of chaos. In this approach, the wavefunction is represented as the sum of several components provided by the network. Specifically, eCPNN learns to generate potential functions in the form of sum-of-products forms that capture spatial electron correlation patterns. The generation process relies on a corresponding encoder-decoder system trained using reinforcement learning, where the reward function corresponds to the total Hamiltonian error. The decoding function then produces the potential terms that minimize this error. Notably, the model is entirely self-supervised and requires no additional data beyond the initial and terminal state measurements. We demonstrate its capability to reproduce time-evolution dynamics aligned with exact full-configuration interaction methods for atoms including Argon, Manganese, and others. The methodology is further extended to test the generation of real-time Gaussian stochastic trajectories that reflect quantum behavior under varying levels of decoherence.

This study presents a method for object pose estimation that leverages the stable spatial relationships among part segments. Traditional approaches relying on direct point-to-point matching between 3D CAD models and 2D images often falter in difficult scenarios due to occlusions, narrow fields of view, or inaccurate initial poses. To mitigate these issues, we propose enhancing local features by aggregating them across a local area, arguing that consistent visual-geometric correspondences are more readily detectable for candidate part regions than for individual points. Consequently, we introduce ProjectGroup, an End-to-End Pipeline designed for efficient and robust feature learning for object parts. Our methodology comprises two main components: Part-by-Area Matching, utilized for robust part detection, and Visual-Geometric Part-Synced Augmentedmentation, which enhances visual features by integrating accurate 2D projections of corresponding 3D parts during training. Comprehensive evaluations on the PoseBench and TotalTexture datasets confirm that our approach significantly surpasses state-of-the-art benchmarks regarding both robustness and spatial invariance. Our source code and POSed parts-based pretrained models are available at https://github.com/Kong-K/ProjectGroup/tree/main.

Few-shot learning (FSL) has gained significant traction in domains like computer vision due to its ability to handle tasks requiring minimal data. However, FSL performance frequently degrades when encountering outlier samples, and while outlier detection has been studied extensively in supervised and self-supervised deep learning, these methods are not feasible in the few-shot setting because they rely on large datasets for robust feature extraction. This paper introduces a novel framework named Sub-Network Based Outlier Detection for FSL (SNOT-Net), which allows for efficient and effective outlier identification within this constrained setting. Specifically, the proposed method extracts shared task-agnostic features utilizing an auxiliary sub-network and computes an anomaly score by comparing these anomaly metrics against the average similarity of common task-specific prototypes. Conversely, SNOT-In, the module responsible for average anomaly similarity, enhances overall learning accuracy, thereby boosting performance across tasks, particularly those with overlapping features and low intra-class variance.

We implemented a lightweight tool, DoableRec, which extracts business structures from standard knowledge graphs and configures the underlying GNN. Evaluations using three real-world datasets demonstrate that our method not only outstrips previous state-of-the-art baselines but also achieves superior performance compared to specialized application-tailored settings.

Creating realistic conversations, even on a limited scale like several turns, remains a major challenge in natural language processing. To address this, we introduce a new task for multi-turn dialog generation grounded in a "theory of mind" (ToM). Based on psychological research, this extended challenge requires basic ToM capabilities, specifically inferring another's intentions and beliefs about the real-world environment from context. We evaluate three baseline deep learning approaches and release three powerful teacher-student neural networks trained sequentially with progressive ToM enhancements; these proposed models serve as comparators. Our results demonstrate a significant increase in environmental awareness and factual consistency across generated responses relative to standard baselines, reliably capturing both second- and first-order ToM. Future directions will explore how further advanced ToM reasoning can be integrated to handle increased levels of complexity.

We examine the dynamics and movement of nearest-neighbor dimers on both the triangular (T) and diamond (DD) lattice geometries, which serve as alternative forms of the triadic lattice. By evaluating the triadic Heisenberg antiferromagnet—constrained by either dimers or triadic interactions—under periodic boundary conditions within a one-dimension variant across multiple lattice forms, we derive exact solutions for the ground-state energy, corresponding eigenvalues forming the energy spectrum, and their respective wave functions as functions of lattice configuration. Furthermore, we explore physical behaviors associated with these models: specific manifestations of Cooper-like pair phenomena in one-dimension infinite boundary conditions and phase transitions resulting from competing phase scenarios between dimerized and triagnetic lattice forms. Notably, transitions between A and B lattice forms exhibit distinct characteristics depending on whether they are induced by a dimerization parameter variation or an interaction strength change. These transitions, occurring across the critical threshold separating the Nérel and ferromagnet lattice forms, may present distinct features when traversing the boundary due to differences arising from the underlying lattice geometry. Finally, we analyze the quantum phase of the system near critical transition thresholds through an examination of the von Neumann entropy associated with a sub-partitioned dimeric unit.

In this framework, the primary dark matter consists of thermalized active neutrinos from the early Universe that lose their mass via the gradual formation of a high-scale potential well, similar to the mechanism observed in pion physics. However, this potential also admits tiny thermal fluctuations, similar to the de Sitter case, which allow an secondary dark matter component to form by producing pairs of neutrinos. We identify this secondary component as the ultralight dark matter, generated through such production mechanisms. Because these two components together constitute dark matter, a crucial constraint is maintaining equality of their halo-scale masses. We further demonstrate using a simple model where the potential is proportional to the neutrino flavor eigenstates rather than just neutrinos alone allows us to evade structure bounds even at smaller coupling values.

Creating meaningful and diverse content in response-to-grounded dialogue systems is challenging, particularly when a single prompt must elicit varied answers. In this work, using real-world dialogue datasets as inspiration, aim to enhance both semantic diversity and quality of responses within a fixed contextual window (e.g., Chameleon dataset with BACH character responses). Existing methods often increase diversity by encouraging exploration of novel conceptual dimensions; however, this can lead to lower overall quality or the generation of implausible responses. To address these drawbacks, we propose SimpleConcept, a method that directs a Large Language Model toward underutilized conceptual territories during sampling, without sacrificing existing response standards. By calculating the frequency of existing concepts in current generation history and penalizing their recurrence, our approach encourages the exploration of dormant semantic dimensions. Evaluation results demonstrate SimpleConcept's superiority over baseline techniques in multilingual settings across four metrics: Blue, ROUGE-L, Multilingual BART-Score, and Multilingual ROUGE-M.

Automated assistance and advanced driving technologies are increasingly dependent on monitoring traffic participants, relying on sensor-based systems to maintain safety and reliability under various environmental conditions. Existing methods for recognizing human actions typically achieve superior accuracy with extensive, synchronized multi-camera setups, processing vast data volumes to achieve results. Conversely, critical tasks such as detecting traffic participants only need to identify specific human actions, making high-volume multi-view processing unnecessary and introducing significant latency. Addressing this, we have developed a novel, end-to-end traffic participant action recognition framework that enhances system robustness by leveraging conditionality within multi-view sensor inputs for detection and processing. This intelligent conditionally approach enables the effective use of multiple sensor streams during actual inference. Furthermore, we introduced an optical flow conditional selection mechanism. This mechanism determines whether to leverage flow data from one or multiple views based on visibility conditions, ensuring optimal performance even when optical blockage hinders the detection of actions in more views.

Score calibration is a prevalent technique for enhancing the performance of imbalanced classification models. These methods adjust the output of the corresponding "inherent" balanced model to better reflect true class probabilities by re-estimating class-specific probability thresholds at a given decision level. This study provides an in-depth theoretical examination of how various score calibration approaches impact deep learning models. Our research highlights two crucial insights: first, these methods are highly sensitive to the model's inherent classification error and second, they exhibit distinct performance disparities based on whether the input data follows a balanced or imbalanced distribution as long as the underlying error varies. Building on these findings, we devise a novel framework to develop balanced data representations using a threshold-dependent clustering method to induce balanced distributions and improved boundary separation, effectively allowing standard calibration techniques to attain optimal accuracy. We validate this approach on nine datasets ranging from relatively balanced to extremely skewed, demonstrating significant improvements in both deep classification tasks and binary hypothesis testing over current state-of-the-art solutions.

Developing control strategies for bipedal robots is hampered by the combinatorial explosion of possible movements. While open-loop pre-recorded trajectories are easily generated, these robots typically falter once perturbations arise, necessitating a shift toward closed-loop feedback control for robust and adaptable locomotion. In this study, we demonstrate that certain feedback structures allow for a tractable, exhaustive enumeration. Specifically, we define a categorical feedback class known as Monotonic Velocity Line (VMl) control and utilize a novel methodology to populate the manifold of feasible gains within less than one hour. By applying this approach, we achieved a dynamically stable walking sequence for the 7-degree-of-freedom HeHe robot on flat terrain. Furthermore, the algorithm required approximately 28 hours to reject all ineffective gains when testing on rugged terrain, thereby confirming the practical viability of this technique.

The flux through a planar surface is often estimated using discrete samples from a domain extending beyond the surface into infinity. When samples are taken at fixed intervals, the resulting estimation error vector exhibits specific structures: under white noise, the error components are independent and share equal variance; conversely, with linear noise correlation, the error components remain independent but variances differ. This paper provides a methodology to optimize sample placement by minimizing error variance within an infinite domain. Achieved via the Chapman-Kolmogorov equations, these optimization strategies yield sample configurations that are nearly equal in performance regardless of the duration of noise correlation. Furthermore, when noise correlation decays beyond linear limits—making the measurements more independent—specific and closed-form solutions for optimal sample positions are derived. For both noise types, incorporating sample weights significantly improves flux estimation accuracy compared to unweighted methods, with weighted schemes under linear noise correlation attaining accuracy levels exceeding those possible if the noise were treated as uncorrelated and of uniform variance.

Modern data analytics heavily relies on the rapid processing of real-time, high-dimensional streams. While numerous datastream execution engines are available, configuring their various components to maximize performance remains a difficult task that typically requires extensive manual tuning and access to static datasets. In this study, we introduced 'LifeStream', a unified framework designed to simultaneously optimize components dataflow engines. 'LifeStream' eliminates the need for complex, static 'black-box' optimizations by adopting an iterative approach using live stochastic techniques, commonly used in engineering. By continuously measuring end-to-end performance on actual streams rather than static data, this framework simplifies tuning into a reliable, 'white-box' process that is easy to implement across different environments and resolvers, even when multiple data sources vary simultaneously in stream characteristics. In extensive tests covering both recurring and unique data types from leading benchmarks, including dataflow environments like Apache Flink and Apache Spark, we show that LifeTune successfully outperforms the best hand-optimized configurations found in numerical libraries when processing both static and high-dimensional streams; specifically, our method achieves significantly faster results on live streams compared to these manual benchmarks.

BiAM consists of three main modules: a Self-Attention layer that refines speech byte-level sequences by capturing long-distance connections within audio data; Bidirectional Attention (BA), which jointly encdecemes both speech representations and linguistic information; and a Concat module designed to combine information from both directions of attention. Therefore, combining big data-driven neural models with BiAM has the potential to further boost automated call comprehension performance.

Recent advancements in Natural Language Processing (NLL) and Computer science have yielded models that appear to handle negation-like semantic tasks in Named Entity Recognition (NER) and Natural Inference (NLI) tasks at or even exceeding human performance levels. To address this gap, this paper introduces formal definitions for entity and sentence levels of negation along with specific types for each. We propose two tasks covering entity and sentence levels, respectively: Entity-Negated NER (ENNER) and Not-Phenomena Sentences (NOS). Both tasks have been used to build test sets for ENNER and NOS for entity and sentences, respectively. To assess performance on these tasks, we report errors in ENNER as failing to remove a correct entity mention or including an incorrect one, and errors in NOS as misclassifying the negation status of a sentence. Under our metrics, NLL performance drops dramatically compared to prior studies, and human performance is significantly better supported. Model performance on NOS is specifically affected, showing that current approaches are not adequate for such complex negation. These results suggest new paths forward for addressing negation challenges across NLL systems and modeling.

The findings in the paper contribute by demonstrating that when research moves from examining one model in isolation to contrasting both models with their respective representations of inequality, there are distinct and meaningful shifts in how the public policies should be designed.

Researchers, developers, and product owners frequently face the challenge of identifying incorrect or flawed data within machine learning (ML) pipelines. Conventional strategies typically rely on random data sampling and threshold metrics to estimate these issues, a process that is both sluggish and imprecise. To address this gap, we present DataScope, an interactive system that leverages aggregate statistics and visualizations to facilitate rapid data debugging. Note that DataScope requires no access to raw data and remains privacy-preserving. By enhancing efficiency for debugging both public and private datasets at various granularities, the system accelerates the identification of problematic areas and accelerates decision-making regarding data acceptance or rejection for ML training purposes, all while maintaining confidentiality. Through empirical evaluations across three corporate privacy contexts and three data benchmarks, the results indicate that DataScope offers significantly superior issue detection accuracy and efficiency compared to industry-standard baselines. Specifically, the system delivers issues detection accuracies 20% to 80% higher than comparisons and reduces the time required for reporting at the record levels by between 7% and 93% at equivalent detail degrees, thereby enhancing the capacity for efficient exploration and robust verification of data integrity.

We introduce Shared Individual Trajectories (SIT), a novel experience sharing mechanism designed for Markov Decision Processes (MDPs) that are shared among multiple agents in a way that remains fair and effective. The core challenge in achieving this lies in determining what data to transmit and how to transmit it, particularly when considering the risks of overwriting individual experiences and potential biases toward dominant agents. Quantum error correction is essential for scaling up fault-tolerant quantum computers, but constructing useful codes and assessing their error correction capabilities present significant challenges because optimal strategies depend on inaccessible information, such as the ideal logical state. In this work, we evaluate quantum hardware for code construction and error analysis by focusing on a prototypical two-dimensional stabilizer code known as the toric code on a torus (T2C). We derive an analytical solution for optimal quantum circuit error correction applied to T2C, an ideal benchmark since solutions are unobtainable for most other codes. Specifically, we determine the set of "threshold surfaces," which define how discrete amplitude and phase error rates affect the ability to surpass a specific continuous entropy threshold for both code T2C and its Klein bottle variant in this optimal scenario. Although these results are most meaningful for the T2C benchmark, they also yield insights regarding general quantum hardware development and error assessment.

This study examines an enhanced encoding scheme for user feedback in the downlink, where the base station (BS) utilizes clustered codebooks to transmit user indices. Unlike traditional approaches where users belong to fixed clusters formed by Lloyd clustering with a pilot count equal to the number of clusters—imposing excessive pilot overhead—this proposed method employs a dynamic, data-driven clustering strategy where the BS only needs to broadcast cluster IDs. Users follow the precoding patterns corresponding to their assigned IDs, and clusters evolve every coherence interval to optimize the sum mean-squared error (MSE) at the BS based on recent channel states. Attaining this dynamic clustering is computationally lighter than forcing all users into a single super-cluster. Furthermore, if the number of clusters remains fixed, this mechanism significantly reduces feedback overhead compared to conventional methods. In the dynamic scenario where clusters adjust both in size and number per interval, we present a suboptimal yet efficient clustering algorithm. Simulation outcomes demonstrate that this feedback approach barely incurs any performance degradation in terms sum MSE when an optimal or near-optimal clustering algorithm is used.

Connected Automated Vehicles (CAVs) benefit from precise, high-resolution traffic signal data, which is essential for safe and efficient navigation at urban intersections. This study tackles the challenge of trajectory optimization for CAVs approaching a four-way intersection while dealing with various signal and road conditions, including the critical moments of phase transitions. We establish a comprehensive framework that integrates a detailed traffic light model, kinetic constraints, a detailed vehicle dynamics system, and an cost function to generate optimal trajectories. A model predictive control (MPC) algorithm is employed to solve the resulting optimal control problem, with a detailed analysis focused on phase changes for yellow and red phases to refine the cost function and constraints for enhanced accuracy. To demonstrate the approach's viability, we simulate three scenario types: generating optimal paths at intersection entry, execution paths within the intersection, and safe emergency braking maneuvers. The resulting trajectories are confirmed through co-simulation with dynamic traffic light environment models, ensuring robustness and realistic vehicle behavior.

Lobster-eye optics offer a promising avenue for X-ray telescope development by utilizing a "super-pixel" imaging mechanism, where each pixel corresponds to one super-pixel and reflects an image of the super-pixel's dividing structure. As the target turns, a "plus" sign appears in each super-pixel; however, due to reflection limitations, only one "arm"—referred to as a "leg"—is visible at any given moment within a single frame. We established a mapping between distinct legs of the cross and specific super-pixels, determining that approximately 15 degrees of rotational precision suffices to distinguish between them. Collectively, these results indicate that this approach provides an effective and practical method for identifying super-pixels in a lobster-eye telescope.

Graph Neural Networks constitute a class of algorithms designed to analyze graph-structured data. Since their introduction, significant effort has been dedicated to developing tractable models within the space of hyperbolic geometry to effectively capture the multi-scale, tree-like structures inherent in such data. Our method utilizes geodesic distances to construct a local neighborhood definition and employs geodesic features to compute aggregation functions, eliminating the dependency on Euclidean node features commonly used in graph convolutional operations. We provide theoretical proof demonstrating that our method produces aggregation results that retain local geodesic neighborhood structures more faithfully, offering a more efficient and practical solution for graph classification tasks compared to the latest hyperbolic GCN model. Experiments across three datasets confirm LGCN's superior performance relative to both Euclidean and hyperbolic graph convolutional baselines, with an additional module learning analysis supporting these findings and performance levels.

Utilizing generative adversarial networks (GANs) to construct counterfactuals is a prominent technique for enhancing and assessing predictive models through data augmentation. However, the ability of condition-based modification in image-only modality models to reflect genuine pathological realities remains questionable, as most existing approaches learn mappings from image pixels directly without explicit domain knowledge. This research evaluates the capacity of counterfactuals generated by learned codes in latent spaces to represent true medical semantics by conducting a case study on a disease detection task within domain-specific datasets (e.g., Dermatology and Radiology). Our findings indicate that models trained on augmented data utilizing latent code manipulations exhibit actual improvements in disease detection capabilities when evaluated on held-out data, with evidence from gradient-based probing suggesting that added data enhances the semantic clarity of disease features. These results were specific to models capable of separating common background characteristics from condition-specific anomalies, leading to a proposed method, called Disentangled Latent Code Modification (LCM), applicable across various subdomains of medical imaging.

Multidimensional data is ubiquitous across diverse fields, yet conveniently and interactively visualizing such data graphically remains challenging, particularly when conveying the statistical interdependencies of variables. We present "DataArtist," a new application called "DataArtist," designed to simplify and streamline the visualization of multidimensional data dependencies in an appealing and user-friendly manner. Specifically, "DataArtist" focuses on rendering beautiful parallel coordinates diagrams by automatically generating aesthetically refined color palettes for this purpose; it achieves this by offering expert-level guidance throughout the entire data exploration process. The application requires no specialized statistical knowledge and offers two distinct automatic coloring strategies. The first, "DaExpert," leverages advanced Gnostic techniques, while the second, "DaArtist," utilizes machine learning algorithms. Both methods efficiently analyze local and global data characteristics across all dimensions and synthesize these insights to produce optimal color configurations for parallel coordinates diagrams. Additionally, both strategies support the customization of specific aspects via user feedback, such as adjusting individual variable weight significance. Extensive evaluations across datasets with varying data artist approaches and evaluation methods demonstrate the system's efficacy, and field studies reveal that this application enhances exploration capabilities while facilitating quicker and more informed understanding of data relationships.
